clinicalPearls: Abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta before delivery, classically presenting with painful vaginal bleeding and a tender, firm, or hypertonic uterus
Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the degree of vaginal blood loss can badly underestimate the true haemorrhage
Risk factors include hypertension and pre-eclampsia, trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, polyhydramnios with rapid decompression, and thrombophilia
Fetal compromise or death can occur rapidly because the separated placenta cannot support gas exchange
It is largely a clinical diagnosis; ultrasound is insensitive and a normal scan does not exclude abruption
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is an important complication, particularly with large abruptions or fetal demise
Management depends on maternal and fetal status: resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often by caesarean) when there is fetal distress or maternal instability
Anti-D should be given to rhesus-negative women and blood products used to correct coagulopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Abruption begins with rupture of maternal decidual vessels, causing bleeding into the decidua basalis that splits the placenta from the uterine wall. The expanding retroplacental clot further separates the placenta, reducing the functional area for maternal-fetal exchange and provoking uterine irritability and contraction. Thromboplastins released from the disrupted placenta and decidua enter the maternal circulation and can trigger consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation), while extravasation of blood into the myometrium (Couvelaire uterus) impairs contractility and postpartum haemostasis.
additionalDifferentials: Local genital tract causes of bleeding
Acute abdomen from a non-obstetric cause
additionalInvestigations: Continuous cardiotocography to detect fetal compromise and uterine hypertonicity
Full blood count and serial haemoglobin
Coagulation screen including fibrinogen to identify disseminated intravascular coagulation
Ultrasound mainly to exclude praevia rather than to confirm abruption
Kleihauer test in rhesus-negative women to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage
redFlags: Maternal haemodynamic instability or shock, which may be disproportionate to visible blood loss due to concealed haemorrhage
Non-reassuring or absent fetal heart activity
Developing coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen and abnormal clotting
A rigid, exquisitely tender uterus with frequent contractions
Rapid clinical deterioration requiring emergency delivery
reference.prognosis: Small abruptions with a stable mother and reassuring fetus may allow expectant management with good outcomes. Large abruptions carry high risks of fetal death, maternal haemorrhage, coagulopathy, and organ injury, and abruption is a leading cause of perinatal mortality and antepartum stillbirth. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is increased.
pitfalls: Being falsely reassured by minimal external bleeding when concealed haemorrhage is severe
Relying on ultrasound to rule out abruption
Delaying delivery in the face of fetal distress or maternal instability
Failing to consider abruption after seemingly minor abdominal trauma in pregnancy
